--- title: Faster training author: Marie-Hélène Burle --- :::{.def} [The training loop](pt2_loop.qmd) of the previous section is modern and complete, but it runs exactly as written: one Python-level operation at a time. This section covers the standard levers that make a working loop fast: `torch.compile`, reduced-precision matrix math, the profiler that tells you where the time actually goes, and the arithmetic that tells you whether a model fits on a GPU. ::: ## Setup ::: {#2d4aa042 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import time # to time epochs import torch from torch import nn from torch.utils.data import DataLoader, Subset from torchvision.datasets import EuroSAT from torchvision.transforms import v2 as T ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: ## A baseline epoch Here is the timing harness for this page: one warmup epoch (worker startup, CUDA context, caches), then one timed epoch at steady state: ::: {#d4804be0 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} def timed_epoch(m): """Run one epoch of bare training steps on model m, return seconds.""" t0 = time.perf_counter() for x, y in train_loader: x = x.to(device, non_blocking=True) y = y.to(device, non_blocking=True) optimizer.zero_grad() loss = loss_fn(m(x), y) loss.backward() optimizer.step() torch.accelerator.synchronize() return time.perf_counter() - t0 ``` ::: ::: {#718643ef .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} timed_epoch(model) # warmup print(f"eager: {timed_epoch(model):4.1f} s") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: This is eager PyTorch: each operation is launched one at a time, exactly as the code is written. On small models like ours, the accelerator spends much of each step waiting for the next kernel launch: the model is so small that its 95,000 parameters cannot keep the hardware busy. ## torch.compile [`torch.compile`](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/generated/torch.compile.html) wraps a module so that its first call captures the operations into a graph, which is then compiled into fused kernels and optimized as a whole: ::: {#401c6664 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} compiled = torch.compile(model) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: Two things to read in these numbers: - The first epoch pays a one-time compilation cost, typically tens of seconds for a model this size. The compiled artifacts are cached on disk (under [Triton]{.codelike}'s cache directory), so a later process that compiles the same graph starts faster. - From the second epoch on, the compiled model runs the same training step faster than eager. How much faster varies a lot: our CNN interleaves convolutions with small elementwise operations, and fusing those helps, but the big convolutions were already well served by cuDNN. Models with more Python-level overhead (transformers are the classic) see larger gains. :::{.note} **What happens under the hood?** Two things. First, [TorchDynamo](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/dynamo.html) records the operations your Python code performs on the model into a graph (stopping at "graph breaks" it cannot handle, and compiling each fragment). Second, the [Inductor](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/inductor.html) backend generates optimized kernels for that graph: [Triton](https://github.com/openai/triton) kernels on GPUs. Fusing sequences of elementwise operations into one kernel is where much of the speedup comes from: fewer launches, and intermediate results stay in fast GPU memory. ::: :::{.note} **Watch out for recompilations.** A graph is compiled for the shapes it sees. Our training loader yields batches of shape `(64, 3, 64, 64)` all the way, except the last one, which has 32 images: the first epoch compiles the model twice. With many distinct shapes (variable sequence lengths, varying image sizes), `torch.compile` can spend its time recompiling instead of training. Two remedies: `drop_last=True` on the training loader ([we met the option](pt2_dataloaders.qmd) when counting batches), and `torch.compile(model, dynamic=True)` to compile shape-generic graphs. ::: `torch.compile` also takes a `mode` argument: the default balances compile time against speed, while `mode="max-autotune"` lets the compiler try more kernel variants at the cost of longer compilation. For a loop that runs for hours, a few extra minutes of compilation are a good trade. ## TF32 The compute that dominates training is matrix multiplication, and GPUs have fast units for it. Since the Ampere generation (2020), NVIDIA GPUs can run float32 matrix products in [TF32](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/notes/cuda.html#tf32-on-nvidia-ampere-and-later), a format that keeps float32's range but carries only 10 bits of mantissa. The accuracy loss is invisible for deep learning, and the speedup on matmul-heavy workloads is substantial. | Format | Sign | Exponent | Mantissa | Notes | | :--- | :---: | :---: | :---: | :--- | | float32 | 1 | 8 | 23 | the default dtype of training | | TF32 | 1 | 8 | 10 | float32 range, reduced precision, used internally by tensor cores | | bfloat16 | 1 | 8 | 7 | [the autocast format of our loop](pt2_loop.qmd) | PyTorch lets you pick how float32 matmuls are allowed to degrade: ::: {#2f6875f7 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(torch.get_float32_matmul_precision()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: The default, `"highest"`, never leaves float32. `"high"` allows TF32 (or bfloat16 on hardware without TF32), and `"medium"` allows bfloat16. Convolutions have a separate switch, `torch.backends.cudnn.allow_tf32`, which has been `True` by default for years. ```{.python} torch.set_float32_matmul_precision("high") # one line, usually near the top of a script ``` :::{.note} TF32 needs Ampere or newer. The RTX 2060 this page renders on is a Turing GPU: no TF32 units, so the setting changes nothing here, and [our bf16 gate](pt2_loop.qmd) keeps autocast off for the same reason. On the cluster GPUs of the later sections, both switches open and the same code speeds up. ::: ## Profiling Before optimizing anything longer than a page, measure. [torch.profiler](https://pytorch.org/docs/stable/profiler.html) records what each part of a step costs: which kernels ran, for how long, on which device. ::: {#caf0e887 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} import os from torch.profiler import ProfilerActivity, profile os.environ["KINETO_LOG_LEVEL"] = "100" # silence the profiler's own logging x, y = next(iter(train_loader)) x, y = x.to(device), y.to(device) for _ in range(3): # warmup: the first step always runs extra one-time work loss = loss_fn(model(x), y) loss.backward() optimizer.zero_grad() activities = [ProfilerActivity.CPU] if device.type == "cuda": activities.append(ProfilerActivity.CUDA) with profile(activities=activities, record_shapes=True) as prof: for _ in range(5): optimizer.zero_grad() loss = loss_fn(model(x), y) loss.backward() optimizer.step() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: How to read the table: - Each row aggregates all calls to one operation. **Self CPU/CUDA** is the time spent in the operation itself; **CPU total / CUDA total** includes its children. Look at the *self* columns to find the actual hot spots. - `Self CPU %` often shows a large `cudaLaunchKernel`-ish share in small models: the CPU issuing work faster than the GPU? No: the CPU *waiting* to issue the next launch. That is the overhead `torch.compile` reduces. - `CUDA total` empty while `CPU total` is large marks code that runs on the CPU: a sign that something (data manipulation, a metric computed on CPU tensors) silently left the accelerator. The table answers "which operation"; for "called from where", export a trace and open it in a trace viewer: ```{.python} prof.export_chrome_trace("trace.json") # then open https://ui.perfetto.dev ``` :::{.note} The profiler only sees what runs inside its context: our snippet reuses one batch to keep the trace focused on compute, so the data pipeline of the [DataLoaders section](pt2_dataloaders.qmd) is invisible here. For a data-starved run, the diagnosis tools of that section (epoch times, `nvidia-smi`) come first. ::: ## The memory side Speed is one constraint; memory ([VRAM](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_random-access_memory)) is the other. Training a model keeps several copies of the parameters in GPU memory, and knowing their sizes tells you at a glance what fits. For a model trained in float32 with an adaptive optimizer like AdamW: ::: {#cc473567 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} def training_footprint(n_params): """Approximate VRAM for the learned state of a model in MiB.""" per_param = ( 4 # weights + 4 # gradients + 4 + 4 # AdamW keeps two moments per parameter ) return n_params * per_param / 2**20 n_ours = sum(p.numel() for p in model.parameters()) print(f"our CNN: {n_ours:>10,} params ~{training_footprint(n_ours):6.1f} MiB") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: ::: Two conclusions: - Both models fit easily in the 6 GiB of the laptop GPU this course renders on. Add activations (the intermediate results of the forward pass, which scale with batch size), and ResNet-18 training at batch 64 still stays in the neighbourhood of a couple of GiB. - The arithmetic explains when models stop fitting: a 7-billion-parameter model trained in float32 with AdamW needs about 104 GiB for weights, gradients, and moments alone, before a single activation. No single GPU holds that; splitting the training state across several of them is the topic of [a later section](pt2_fsdp.qmd). :::{.note} To measure rather than estimate on a CUDA GPU, read the allocator's high-water mark after a training step: ```{.python} torch.cuda.reset_peak_memory_stats() # then run one step print(f"peak: {torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated() / 2**20:.0f} MiB") ``` Note that mixed precision does not halve this footprint: with autocast, weights, gradients, and optimizer state stay in float32; only the compute runs in bf16. ::: ## Where to start In the order that pays off the soonest: 1. **Feed the accelerator** ([previous section](pt2_dataloaders.qmd)): workers, prefetching, pinned memory. No code change in the model. 2. **`torch.compile`**: one line, meaningful gains on most models, first-call compilation cost. 3. **Precision**: TF32 where available, bf16 autocast otherwise ([the gate of our loop](pt2_loop.qmd)). 4. **More hardware**: when one GPU is genuinely not enough, [the cluster sections](pt2_cluster.qmd) take over. And measure between steps: the profiler for compute, epoch times for the big picture. ::::{.exo} :::{.yourturn} Your turn: ::: Compile with `mode="max-autotune"` and compare the steady-state epoch time with the default mode. Then add `drop_last=True` to the training loader and check that the recompilation for the small final batch disappears from the first epoch. - Hint: `max-autotune` compiles for noticeably longer; watch the first epoch's total time versus the second. ::::
